# 4. Empirical methods

Sections 2 and 3 established what the credit indicator measures and the environment in which it is measured. Credit use is uncommon, involving `r fmt_pct(objs$treatment$share_treated, 1)` of farm households; users are younger and better educated than non-users (Table 1); lending is increasingly intermediated through groups; most loans are not reported as farm loans; and the modal non-applicant reports no need for a loan (Table 3). A method that simply compared output per hectare between borrowers and non-borrowers would fold together three distinct things: differences in the production technology the two groups operate, differences in how well each group uses its own technology, and differences in who borrows. This section sets out how the analysis separates them. Section 4.1 states the mechanisms and the hypotheses they imply. Section 4.2 presents the meta-stochastic frontier that decomposes performance into technology and efficiency. Section 4.3 describes the matching that removes compositional differences on observables. Section 4.4 states what the resulting estimates do and do not identify, and Section 4.5 describes inference and the robustness programme.

## 4.1 Conceptual framework and hypotheses

Credit enters crop production through the liquidity constraint. A farm household that cannot borrow must finance seed, fertilizer, agro-chemicals and hired labour from its own savings or current income, at the point in the season when those resources are scarcest, and must bear the full downside risk of any investment it makes. That position is not incidental: the seasonality, spatial dispersion and covariate risk of rainfed cropping are the material conditions under which credit and insurance markets in tropical smallholder agriculture remain thin, interlinked or absent, so the terms on which a farm can finance a season are a structural feature of the production environment rather than a household-specific accident [@Binswanger1986]. Credit can relax this constraint along two conceptually distinct margins. It can finance lumpy or indivisible investments, such as improved planting material, mechanized services or a switch of crop, that change the technology the farm operates; and it can finance the timely purchase of divisible inputs within a given technology, allowing the farm to operate nearer to the frontier of that technology [@Guirkinger2008; @Kumar2013; @Dessie2015]. The metafrontier framework of Section 4.2 is chosen because it maps onto this distinction: the technology gap ratio (TGR) measures the productive capacity of the technology a group operates relative to the best practice observed in the sample, and technical efficiency (TE) measures how close a farmer comes to the frontier of the group's own technology. The Ghanaian evidence reviewed in Section 1 is mixed in part because it does not make this separation, since each of those studies estimates a single frontier for borrowers and non-borrowers and cannot distinguish a lower efficiency score from a different technology.

From the liquidity-constraint view we derive three hypotheses, stated so that the data can reject them. The first concerns the technology margin. If borrowing finances technology-embodying investment, the frontier of credit users should lie closer to the metafrontier than the frontier of non-users, so that credit use is associated with a higher TGR (H1). The second concerns the efficiency margin. Adoption financed by credit can outrun the agronomic knowledge, risk management and timely input delivery needed to use new inputs well, and repayment obligations can divert management attention or labour toward the activities that generate cash, so that borrowers, conditional on their own technology, produce farther below their frontier; evidence from Ghanaian cocoa shows how much the payoff to new practices depends on complementary training [@Tsiboe2016], and the case for bundling finance with agronomic and risk-management support rests on the same logic [@Barrett2022; @Meyer2015]. We therefore hypothesize that credit use is associated with lower TE (H2), while noting that theory does not exclude the opposite sign, since credit can also permit inputs to be applied at the agronomically appropriate time and can loosen the risk-induced under-application that characterizes poor households facing uninsured consumption risk [@Dercon2011]. The third concerns the shape of the technology rather than the distance to it. Where credit finances working capital, it should raise the output response to the inputs whose timing is most sensitive to liquidity, land preparation and labour, more than to fertilizer, whose contribution is bounded by input quality and application practice that finance alone does not relax; we therefore expect credit users' frontier to be more responsive to land and labour than to fertilizer, relative to non-users (H3). H1 and H2 are tested on the sign and significance of the credit-minus-no-credit differences in TGR and TE (Tables 4 and 5), and H3 on the differences in group-frontier elasticities (Table 4).

Two considerations visible in Section 3 temper the first hypothesis and make its sign an empirical question. Credit relaxes the farm's liquidity constraint only if the loan, or the liquidity it frees, reaches the farm. Loans are fungible [@Hussain2016], only a minority of loans in these data are reported as taken for agricultural purposes (Table 3), and the treatment records borrowing rather than the ability to borrow, so a non-user who reports no need for a loan is not liquidity-constrained in the sense the theory requires. Who borrows is also not random, since lenders target and households self-select, increasingly through group-based schemes whose membership the survey does not record. If the borrowing households are not, as a group, those investing in farm technology, the TGR contrast can be null, and it can be negative if borrowing is concentrated among households whose farm technology is weaker for reasons the observables do not capture, such as distress borrowing after a shock or lender targeting of particular activities. A rejection of H1 is therefore informative about which of these conditions fails rather than a failure of the framework. Each mechanism also implies where the associations should be strongest, and the design measures those dimensions: complementary human capital should make credit more likely to reach the frontier, so the contrasts are reported by operator gender, age and education (Figure 3); crops differ in the cash-input intensity and lumpiness of their technologies, and regions in market access and in the density of financial infrastructure, so the contrasts are reported by major crop and region (Figure 4); and the interaction between credit and the other dimensions of financial inclusion, which Section 3 shows expanding faster than credit itself, is examined by contrasting households with and without a formal account (Figure 2) and within each of the financial-service categories described in Section 2.2 (Table 6). Because the design is observational (Section 4.4), every hypothesis is tested as an association rather than as an effect. The policy reading differs by outcome: if credit is associated with a narrower technology gap but lower efficiency, the case is for bundling credit with extension, risk instruments and reliable input delivery; if it is associated with a wider gap, the case is for asking what borrowing households are financing and whether the loans on offer are sized and timed for crop production [@DeJanvry2020; @WorldBank2024].

## 4.2 Meta-stochastic frontier analysis

Credit users and non-users may face different financing constraints and, plausibly, operate different production technologies. A single frontier fitted to both groups would fold technology differences into measured inefficiency. We therefore estimate a separate stochastic frontier for each group and benchmark both against a common metafrontier, following the two-step stochastic metafrontier of @Huang2014, which envelops the group-specific stochastic frontiers within a metafrontier that is itself stochastic rather than deterministic, so that the technology gap is an estimated quantity carrying its own error rather than a residual imposed by a deterministic envelope. What the framework delivers is the standard decomposition of producer performance in efficiency and productivity analysis [@Coelli2005]: it separates proximity to the best-practice technology, measured by the technology gap ratio (TGR), from efficiency within the group's own technology, measured by technical efficiency (TE); their product is meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE). Credit status does not enter the frontier as a regressor. It defines the groups, $j \in \{\text{credit user},\ \text{non-user}\}$, and thereby the frontier against which each farmer is assessed, so that the two frontiers are free to differ in every coefficient. This is the framework applied to GLSS data by earlier work on gender, age, crop and ecological differences in Ghanaian crop production [@Adaku2023; @Ansah2023a; @Asravor2024; @Tsiboe2021a], here applied to credit.

For group $j$ the stochastic frontier takes a translog form, which nests the Cobb-Douglas form and allows the input elasticities to vary with the input bundle:

$$
f^{j}(x_{ijt}) = \ln(y_{ijt}) = \beta_{0j}
  + \sum_{k} \beta_{kj}\ln(x_{kijt})
  + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}\sum_{k} \beta_{skj}\ln(x_{kijt})\ln(x_{sijt})
  + \beta_{h}h_{ijt} + v_{ijt} - u_{ijt}
$$

$$
u_{ijt} \sim N^{+}\!\left(0,\ \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{j})\right),\qquad
v_{ijt} \sim N\!\left(0,\ \sigma_{vj}^{2}\right)
\qquad\qquad (1)
$$

Here $y_{ijt}$ is the real value of crop output of the $i$th farm operator in group $j$ in survey round $t$; the inputs $x_{kijt}$ are land, planting material, family labour, hired labour, fertilizer and pesticide; and $h_{ijt}$ contains the frontier shifters, namely the shares of cultivated area under each major crop (crops averaging at least 3% of area, with maize as the base), the survey round and the ecological zone. The two-sided term $v_{ijt}$ captures noise and shocks outside the operator's control and is normal with variance $\sigma_{vj}^{2}$ [@Belotti2013]; the one-sided term $u_{ijt} \ge 0$ is technical inefficiency. We adopt a half-normal distribution for $u_{ijt}$, having encountered convergence problems with other distributions in the group-level estimations; exponential, truncated-normal and Rayleigh alternatives are examined among the robustness checks in Section 5.5 (Fig. S2). The inefficiency variance is heteroskedastic, $\sigma_{u_{ijt}}^{2} = \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{j})$, where $w_{ijt}$ contains the operator's age, schooling and gender, land ownership, mechanization and extension contact, the crop diversification index, fixed effects for ecological zone and survey round, and a constant, following previous work on these data [@Adaku2023; @Ansah2023a; @Asravor2024; @Tsiboe2021a]; $\alpha_{j}$ is estimated separately for each group, so the determinants of inefficiency are themselves allowed to differ between credit users and non-users (Table S4). Credit is excluded from $w_{ijt}$ because it defines the groups. Table S5 defines every variable entering the frontier, the inefficiency term and the matching distance of Section 4.3, with the unit in which it is measured and the sign expected of it. Given the estimated frontier for group $j$, the pure technical efficiency of operator $i$ is the conditional expectation

$$
TE_{ijt} = E\!\left(\exp(-u_{ijt}) \mid \varepsilon_{ijt}\right)
\qquad\qquad (2)
$$

where $\varepsilon_{ijt} = v_{ijt} - u_{ijt}$ is the composed error. In the second step, the frontier output predicted for each farmer from its own group frontier, $\hat{y}_{ijt}$, is pooled across groups and a stochastic metafrontier that envelops the group frontiers is estimated as

$$
f^{M}(x_{ijt}) = \ln(\hat{y}_{ijt}) = \beta_{0M}
  + \sum_{k} \beta_{kM}\ln(x_{kiMt})
  + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}\sum_{k} \beta_{skM}\ln(x_{kiMt})\ln(x_{siMt})
  + \beta_{h}h_{ijt} - u_{Mijt}
\qquad\qquad (3)
$$

where $u_{Mijt} \sim N^{+}(0, \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{M}))$ is strictly positive, so that $f^{j}(x_{ijt}) \le f^{M}(x_{ijt})$ for every group, and the same covariates that scale inefficiency in Equation (1) scale the technology gap. The ratio of group $j$'s frontier to the metafrontier is the technology gap ratio,

$$
TGR_{ijt} = \frac{f^{j}(x_{ijt})}{f^{M}(x_{ijt})} = e^{-u_{Mijt}} \le 1
\qquad\qquad (4)
$$

and meta-frontier technical efficiency decomposes as

$$
MTE_{ijt} = f^{j}(x_{ijt})\left(f^{M}(x_{ijt})\,e^{v_{ijt}}\right)^{-1}
  = TGR_{ijt} \times TE_{ijt}
\qquad\qquad (5)
$$

A TGR below one means that, at the farmer's input bundle, the group's technology yields less output than the best practice observed in the pooled sample; a lower TGR is a larger technology gap. TE measures performance against the group's own frontier and MTE against the common one, so Equation (5) attributes any group difference in MTE to a technology component and an efficiency component, which is the distinction on which H1 and H2 turn: a group can be closer to the metafrontier yet less efficient within its own technology, or the reverse.

Estimation proceeds in the two steps of @Huang2014. First, the group frontiers in Equation (1) are estimated by maximum likelihood on all farmers in each group and TE is obtained from Equation (2). Second, the metafrontier in Equation (3) is estimated by maximum likelihood on the group-frontier predictions, on the matched sample described in Section 4.3 and, for comparison, on the unmatched pooled sample, yielding TGR from Equation (4) and MTE from Equation (5); the enveloping is done by the one-sided term $u_{Mijt}$ rather than by a programming constraint, so the metafrontier is not forced through the extreme predictions of the group frontiers. Because an unrestricted translog need not satisfy monotonicity and quasi-concavity at every observation, the frontiers are also estimated with these regularity conditions imposed; this restricted specification is the one reported in Table 4 and Tables S3 and S4, Table 4 reports the share of observations at which each estimated frontier satisfies the two conditions, and the unrestricted frontier is carried as a robustness variant (Fig. S2). Input elasticities are the first derivatives of the estimated frontiers with respect to each logged input, evaluated at the sample means, and returns to scale (RTS) are their sum [@Coelli2005]. Group-level TGR, TE and MTE are averages of the farmer-level scores within each group, and the difference between credit users and non-users is estimated directly by the same procedure, with its own standard error, rather than by subtracting two rounded means. Three diagnostics precede interpretation and are reported in Section 5.1: residual-skewness tests [@Schmidt1984; @Coelli1995] and a one-sided likelihood-ratio test [@Gutierrez2001] establish that a one-sided inefficiency term is present; a likelihood-ratio test of the group frontiers against a common frontier establishes whether the two groups share a technology, which is the condition under which the metafrontier rather than a single frontier is the right benchmark; and the share of composed-error variance attributable to the one-sided term, $\gamma = \sigma_{u}^{2}/\sigma^{2}$, indicates how much of the unexplained dispersion is systematic.

Two extensions use the same machinery. First, the household credit indicator defines the groups in the preferred specification, and the frontiers are re-estimated under the narrower definitions of Section 2.2, in which the operator alone, the operator's spouse, or another household member holds the loan, each definition fitted as its own pair of group frontiers, to test whether the results depend on whose borrowing is counted (Table 5). Second, heterogeneity in the credit contrast is examined by computing the credit-minus-no-credit difference in TGR, TE and MTE within subgroups defined by operator gender, age and education (Figure 3), major crop and administrative region (Figure 4), and the financial-service indicators of Section 3, including formal account ownership (Figure 2 and Table 6). These within-subgroup differences are computed from the main estimation's operator-level scores rather than from separately estimated frontiers, so they describe where the aggregate contrast is concentrated rather than testing distinct technologies within each subgroup.

## 4.3 Forming comparable pairs of farmers

Three features of the credit indicator could bias a naive comparison of users and non-users: it is self-reported, so recall and social-desirability error can misclassify borrowers; credit is not randomly allocated, so lender targeting and self-selection make borrowers differ from non-borrowers in ways that also affect output; and the treatment can be defined at the household or the operator level. Matching addresses the second of these on observables, the alternative definitions of Section 2.2 address the third, and the first is a measurement problem that no estimator in this paper removes, so we set out its likely direction first.

The classification rests on the household's own account of a loan application and its outcome, and self-reported borrowing is not a neutral measurement instrument in this setting. Recall over a twelve-month window is imperfect, and the error is unlikely to be random: small and informal loans are the ones most likely to go unreported, and they are disproportionately the loans smallholders take [@Guirkinger2008; @Meyer2015]. Reporting may also respond to the interview itself, since having applied and been refused is a less comfortable answer than not having applied. Self-reported financial-access measures of this kind are predictive of the outcomes they are meant to proxy while remaining vulnerable to systematic misreport [@DemirgucKunt2017; @Karlan2017; @Klapper2025]. If the dominant error is to record genuine borrowers as non-users, the comparison group is contaminated with borrowers and the estimated contrast is attenuated toward zero, so the magnitudes reported in Section 5 would if anything be understated. We do not treat them as formal bounds, because misreporting that is itself correlated with farm performance could move the contrast in either direction and the data offer no way to check.

Credit users are not a random draw of farmers. Table 1 shows that they are younger and better educated than non-users (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table1", "Age (years)", 3), 1)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table1", "Age (years)", 2), 1)` years; `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table1", "Education (years)", 3), 1)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table1", "Education (years)", 2), 1)` years of schooling), less likely to own their land and more reliant on hired labour, and the loan outcomes in Table 3 indicate that lenders screen on collateral and trust, so borrowing reflects both lender targeting and farmer self-selection. A metafrontier estimated on the raw pooled sample would envelop two groups drawn from different parts of the covariate space, and the resulting technology gap would confound technology with composition. We therefore estimate the metafrontier in Equation (3) on a matched sample in which each credit user is paired one-to-one with a non-user of similar observed characteristics. The purpose differs from that of matching estimators that impute a missing counterfactual outcome [@Abadie2006; @Abadie2016]: here the pairs form a balanced sample on which the metafrontier is estimated, while the user/non-user split that defines the group frontiers is preserved, an approach taken by earlier metafrontier studies facing similar selection concerns [@Mayen2010; @CrespoCebada2014; @Tiedemann2013; @BravoUreta2021; @Asmare2022]. Pairs are formed only within exact strata of operator gender, survey round, region, ecological zone and rural or urban locality, so that no user is compared with a non-user from a different round, place or gender. Within a stratum, the distance between candidates is computed over the operator's demographics (age, schooling, marital status, religion, ethnicity and relationship to the household head), household composition (size, dependency ratio and female share), production choices (crop diversification and the share of land under each crop), land ownership, and the financial-inclusion index described in Section 2.3, whose indicator set, stratum-specific estimation and rescaling onto a common metric are documented in Note S1. Including the index is deliberate: it means that borrowers are compared with non-borrowers of similar overall engagement with financial services, so that the credit contrast is not a proxy for being banked or insured, dimensions that re-enter as heterogeneity cuts in Figure 2 and Table 6. Observations missing any matching covariate are excluded before pairing, and because matching is one-to-one, the matched sample contains equal numbers of users and non-users and is a small fraction of the pooled sample; the group frontiers in Table 4 are estimated on all users and all non-users, with matching applied at the metafrontier stage, so the resulting contrast describes households that resemble borrowers on the matched characteristics rather than the average non-borrowing farm.

Because the covariates are numerous and of mixed type, we compute the distance under eight metrics: propensity scores from logit, probit, complementary log-log and cauchit models, Euclidean and scaled Euclidean distance, and Mahalanobis and robust Mahalanobis distance [@Rosenbaum2010; @Rosenbaum2020]. Comparing them is not incidental to the design. The model used for the propensity score, the distance metric and the rule that forms the pairs are implementation choices to which a matching estimate is sensitive, and the practical guidance is to settle them on the balance achieved after matching rather than on the estimates they produce [@Caliendo2008]. Balance is assessed for every covariate by the absolute standardized mean difference, the variance ratio and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, whose targets are zero, one and zero respectively [@Rubin2001; @Stuart2010], and the specifications are ranked on a composite of these diagnostics rather than on the frontier results they yield. Fig. S1 reports all three for each matched sample against the unmatched sample. Every matched sample removes most of the imbalance visible in the unmatched sample, which is concentrated in schooling, household size, the crop-share indicators and the ethnic, religious and regional composition of the two groups; residual imbalance after matching is largest for household size and operator age and is reported rather than assumed away. The probit propensity-score specification ranks best on the composite criterion and provides the matched sample used in the main analysis; Section 5.5 reports the estimates under each of the other seven matched samples and under no matching (Fig. S2).

The matched sample also supports a direct comparison of input use that precedes the frontier results. For each of the six frontier inputs, expressed per hectare, and for the real value of output per hectare, we estimate the proportional gap associated with credit as a log-linear treatment effect on the matched pairs, for the matched sample as a whole and separately over the covariate distributions of non-users and of users, with the same jackknife inference as the frontier estimates (Figure 1). These gaps are the input-intensity counterpart of the frontier comparison: the frontiers say how much output a group's technology yields from a given bundle, and Figure 1 says whether credit users in fact apply a different bundle, so that a contrast arising because borrowers operate a different technology can be distinguished from one arising because they use more or less of the same inputs.

## 4.4 What the design identifies

Matching balances the covariates we observe. It cannot balance what the GLSS does not record, and several of the omitted determinants of both borrowing and farm performance are plausibly correlated with one another: managerial ability, risk tolerance [@Dercon2011], the quality and provenance of the land the household farms, wealth held outside the surveyed asset modules, prior relationships with lenders, and standing in the community associations through which group-based lending is intermediated. The last of these is not a remote concern here: as Table 3 shows, group-based microfinance rose from `r tbl_pct("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 2, 1)` of loans between the two rounds, so the mechanism allocating credit is increasingly one whose inputs we do not observe. Selectivity-corrected frontier models could in principle address this, but they require an exclusion restriction, a variable that predicts household borrowing and is credibly unrelated to farm performance, and the GLSS contains none that we are prepared to defend; we do not construct one.

**We therefore interpret the estimated differences in TGR, TE and MTE as associations conditional on observables in a balanced sample, not as causal effects of credit.** Where Section 5 uses the language of gaps, differentials or influence, it should be read in that sense. The direction of any remaining bias is not signed by theory: if lenders select the more capable farmers, or the more capable farmers are those who seek credit, the observed contrasts overstate what credit does for the marginal borrower; if borrowing is concentrated among households under financial stress or diversifying out of farming, they understate it. This matters for how the hypotheses are adjudicated. A rejection of H1 is evidence that borrowing households do not, as a group, operate the best-practice technology; it does not by itself establish that borrowing moved them away from it. Two exhibits speak to the question without resolving it. Table 5 re-estimates the contrast under narrower definitions of who in the household borrowed, and a contrast that is stable across the operator's own loan, a spouse's loan and another member's loan is harder to attribute to operator-specific unobservables. The loan-application row of Table 6 estimates the contrast within households in which the operator applied for a loan, so that credit users are compared with applicants whose household did not obtain one; this is the nearest the data come to a comparison in which demand is held constant, although refusal is itself a lender's judgement and the unfunded comparison group is small.

Three further limits bound the interpretation. First, credit is measured as an indicator of use rather than of access: a household that could borrow on good terms and chose not to is pooled with one that could not borrow at all, so the contrast is between borrowers and non-borrowers rather than between the constrained and the unconstrained. That the modal reason for not applying is "no need" rather than an institutional barrier, at `r tbl_pct("table3", "No need", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "No need", 2, 1)` of non-applicants in the two rounds (Table 3), makes the distinction material, and so does the fact that only `r tbl_pct("table3", "Agricultural", 1, 1)` of loans in 2012/13 were reported as taken for farming: a household counted as a credit user may have borrowed for a purpose that never touched the farm, and the group frontiers characterize the technology of borrowing households whatever the loan was used for. It is also one reason the gaps here need not match those in studies that classify households by a direct elicitation of credit constraints [@Guirkinger2008; @Kumar2013]. Second, the design assumes no interference between units, which is not innocuous when a substantial and rising share of lending is group-based and intermediated through the same communities that supply the comparison group; expanded lending to one household may alter the terms available to its neighbours, in either direction, and theory does not determine the direction of the resulting bias. Third, the data are repeated cross-sections, so the estimates compare households at a point in time rather than tracking the same farm before and after borrowing, and the two rounds describe how the associations differ between 2012/13 and 2016/17, not how any farm's performance changed when it obtained credit; the heterogeneity reported in Section 5.6 is obtained by summarizing the matched-sample scores within subgroups, and those contrasts are descriptive rather than separately identified effects.

## 4.5 Inference and robustness

Standard errors come from a cluster jackknife at the enumeration-area (EA) level, the primary sampling unit of the GLSS. For each survey round we form 100 delete-one-EA replicates; in each replicate one EA is removed, the remaining EAs from both rounds are pooled, and the full pipeline is re-run: the group frontiers in Equation (1) are re-estimated with the regularity conditions imposed, the matching is redone, the metafrontier in Equation (3) is re-estimated, and TE, TGR, MTE, the elasticities, the input and output gaps and the subgroup differences are recomputed. Jackknife standard errors are the dispersion of the replicate estimates, so a single set of standard errors carries the uncertainty from clustered sampling, from matching and from frontier estimation together rather than treating the matched sample as fixed. Because the credit-minus-no-credit differences are recomputed within each replicate, each difference in Tables 4 to 6 and in the figures carries its own jackknife standard error rather than one assembled from the two group estimates. We report two-sided tests on these standard errors, mark significance at the 10%, 5% and 1% levels in the tables, and use the 5% level as the threshold in the text, distinguishing throughout the statistical significance of a difference from its economic size.

Robustness is assessed on the same footing and is organized around the sources of specification dependence identified above. Table 5 re-estimates the contrasts under alternative definitions of which household member holds the credit. Fig. S2 re-estimates the headline TGR, TE and MTE contrasts along six dimensions: the functional form (translog against Cobb-Douglas); the distribution of the inefficiency term (half-normal against exponential, truncated-normal and Rayleigh); the estimator used to recover farmer-level efficiency from the composed error; the aggregation of farmer-level scores into group means (weighted mean, simple mean and median); the matched sample (each of the eight distance metrics and the unmatched sample); and the regularity restrictions (restricted against unrestricted frontiers). Section 5.5 reports which of these choices move the estimates and by how much, and a finding is described as robust only along the dimensions on which it survives.
